Don't be offended when I ask this, but you don't have any idea what happens behind the scenes of the development field, do you?

When you have a project/website that you want to translate to another platform, three things will usually happen. The native project will need to be examined, documented, and et cetera, either piece by piece or at once, the code will need to be actually recreated, and it will need to be tested to make sure it retains all of the old functionality of the older page. It can easily take weeks alone to revise the logic for the site if years of minuscule additions create a confusing, inefficient mess (how much depends on the size of the project and the actual platform. Can't say much for specifics regarding Flash because Team .NET lol). Once this happens, development of the new platform requires developers. This leaves the people in charge of organizing the restructure with three actions: (1) track how many developers already on payroll are capable of developing in the new platform or disciplined only in the old one, (2) balance amount of developers focused on the recreation and developers managing the old project (as shutting down your website for a month (if you're lucky) really isn't smart business-wise in an age where people complain about a one-hour server change) accordingly to make sure that both platforms get the attention they require, and, if this yields a shortage of developers, (3) hire more developers.

Let's forget about testing for a moment, since the amount of resources this consumes may vary drastically, and assume that everything else works out fine. Since us code monkeys at the bottom don't make the call to completely revamp everything, consider how a management position would see this process. You essentially have a long period of time then where the amount of money spent paying programmers could easily double for no apparent outcome that generates little extra revenue when finished. Repeat when the next big thing comes out.
